summary: Teach protractor use as a placement-and-read procedure for measuring and drawing angles in whole-number degrees (Y5, ages 9–10). Learners already know an angle is an amount of turn measured in degrees (a full turn = 360°, so n one-degree turns = n degrees). The hard parts are the SET-UP (vertex exactly on the centre cross, one ray exactly along the 0-line) and CHOOSING which of the two scales to read. Lead with estimation: decide acute/right/obtuse (and roughly how many degrees) before measuring, then use that judgement to pick the scale and sanity-check the read. Meeting a full-circle 360° protractor before the standard two-scale semicircular one keeps the fraction-of-a-turn meaning visible. Target errors: reading the mirror value (133° for 47°), believing the tool only works when a ray is horizontal, judging size by ray length, and not extending short rays.
misconceptions: Reads the wrong scale — lands on the mirror value (e.g. 133° instead of 47°) because the child reads whichever number the ray crosses without checking acute/obtuse.
Believes the protractor only works when a ray is horizontal ('standard position') and cannot measure a rotated angle.
Measures the length of the rays or the gap between their ends rather than the rotation between them (arm-length carryover).
Does not extend rays that fall short of the scale arc, then reads a smaller/ambiguous value or gives up.

activities.title: Estimate-first measuring across orientations
steps: Before touching the protractor, say aloud whether each angle is acute, right, or obtuse, and give a rough degree estimate against benchmarks (30°, 45°, 60°, 90°, 120°, 180°).
Place the protractor so the vertex sits exactly on the centre cross AND one ray lies exactly along the 0-line — check both before reading anything.

Read the OTHER ray on the scale that starts at 0 on the ray you lined up, and check that the number matches your acute/obtuse estimate, then state the measure (e.g. report a rotated angle as 47°, not its mirror value 133°).
Repeat with angles drawn in non-standard orientations: a ray pointing up, down, and diagonally — do not rotate the paper to force a ray horizontal.
When rays are drawn too short to reach the scale arc, extend a ray with a ruler first, then measure; confirm the measure is the same before and after extending.
activities.insight: The measure is the amount of opening between the rays, read once the tool is correctly placed; it does not depend on ray length or on any ray being horizontal. The correct scale is the one that starts at 0 on the aligned ray; the acute/obtuse estimate (checked against the 90° benchmark) is a quick check that the right scale was read. For angles very close to 90° both scales read about the same, so careful placement decides the read.

activities.title: Full-circle before two-scale semicircle
steps: Measure several angles first on a full-circle (360°) protractor, reading the degrees as a fraction of a whole turn.
Then switch to the standard two-scale semicircular protractor and, for each angle, state whether you will read the inner or outer scale and why, before reading it.
Verbalise the link: '90° is a quarter turn; this angle is a bit less than a quarter so it is under 90°.'
activities.insight: Degrees are a fraction of a whole turn; the two scales on a semicircular protractor run in opposite directions, and the acute/obtuse judgement (checked against the 90° benchmark) is the main guide to which one applies — except for angles close to 90°, where both scales read near 90° and careful placement, not the acute/obtuse call, settles the read.

activities.title: Draw then check
steps: To draw a 135° angle: mark the vertex, draw a baseline, place the protractor (vertex on centre, baseline on 0-line).
Count UP the correct scale to 135°, mark a dot, and join the dot to the vertex.
Re-measure the angle you drew and confirm it reads about 135° (within ±2°); redraw if it is off.
Try drawing in a non-horizontal orientation too, so drawing is not tied to a baseline along the bottom of the page.
activities.insight: Drawing an angle is the inverse of measuring one: the same placement and scale-choice skills apply, and re-measuring your own drawing is a built-in check.

activities.title: Reasoning probes and reflex-angle stretch
steps: Compare a rotated angle and a horizontal one and answer 'Which is bigger? How could you be sure without being told?' — justify by measuring, not by orientation.
Answer: 'If these two lines were made twice as long but opened the same, what would the protractor say?' and explain why the measure is unchanged.
Explain why you read one scale and not the other for a given angle.
Attempt to start drawing a 210° angle and explain what happens when the semicircular scale only runs to 180° (reasoning about reflex angles).
activities.insight: A secure measurer justifies readings by the amount of opening and by acute/obtuse scale choice, recognises ray length is irrelevant, and notices the semicircular scale's 180° limit when facing a reflex angle.

checkQuestion: Put three angles in front of the child, each drawn in a DIFFERENT orientation (one with a horizontal ray, one rotated so no ray is horizontal, one with rays drawn too short to reach the protractor's scale). Hand them a protractor and say: 'Measure each of these. Tell me the degrees.' Then give a blank and say: 'Now draw me an angle of exactly 135°.' Watch how they place the tool and choose the scale — do not explain the procedure.
checkAnswer: For each angle: vertex placed on the centre-cross, one ray on the 0-line, reads the scale that matches whether the angle is acute or obtuse (e.g. reports the rotated angle correctly rather than its mirror value), extends the short rays before reading, and reads to within ±2°. For the drawing: marks the vertex and baseline, counts up the correct scale, and draws an angle that re-measures to about 135°.
